title: Architecture Governance That Enables Rather Than Blocks
objectives: Design governance processes that add value without creating bottlenecks
Understand how the RESET framework and Digital Assurance Playbook reshape governance
Establish and run Architecture Review Boards that delivery teams trust
Navigate the relationship between organisational assurance and central GDS oversight
Use the cross-government ADR Framework to create visibility and traceability
whyThisMatters:
Architecture governance has a reputation problem. In too many organisations, it means a committee that meets fortnightly to reject things. Delivery teams learn to avoid it, work around it, or present decisions after they have already been made, turning the governance process into a rubber stamp that adds delay without adding value.

This matters because the alternative — no governance at all — is worse. Without governance, departments duplicate effort, teams make contradictory technology choices, security vulnerabilities accumulate unnoticed, and the overall technology estate becomes incoherent. The National Audit Office has repeatedly identified weak governance as a root cause of failed government technology programmes.

The challenge for architects at this level is designing governance that sits in the productive middle ground: lightweight enough that teams engage willingly, rigorous enough that it catches genuine problems, and strategic enough that it drives coherence across the estate. Since April 2026, the UK government has fundamentally reshaped how digital governance works through the RESET framework and the Digital Assurance Playbook. Understanding this new landscape is essential for any architect operating at senior level.

content.heading: What Governance Actually Means (And What It Does Not)
content.body:
Governance is the system of decision rights, accountability structures, and processes that ensure an organisation's technology investments support its objectives. That definition is deliberately broad because governance is not a single meeting or a single document. It is the entire ecosystem of how technology decisions get made, challenged, recorded, and enforced.

In government, architecture governance operates at three levels:

At the cross-government level, the Technical Design Council (TDC) — established as part of the Blueprint for Modern Digital Government — brings together Chief Technology Officers from across the public sector to make decisions affecting cross-government architecture and shared platforms. The GDS Enterprise Architecture team, relaunched in late 2025 within the Office of the Chief Technology Officer (OCTO), provides strategic direction and architectural coherence across the public sector. Their focus is on harmonisation, interoperability, and reuse.

At the departmental level, each organisation has its own architecture governance — typically an Architecture Review Board (ARB) or Design Authority — that ensures solutions align with departmental strategy, standards, and the wider technology landscape. The composition, authority, and cadence of these bodies varies significantly between departments.

At the programme or service level, architecture decisions are made within delivery teams, governed by sprint ceremonies, technical design sessions, and peer review. The question governance must answer is: which decisions can be made here, and which need to be escalated?

What governance is NOT: it is not a mechanism for architects to control delivery teams. It is not a veto power. It is not a bureaucratic hurdle designed to slow things down. When governance becomes any of these things, it has failed — not because the principle is wrong, but because the implementation is wrong.

content.heading: The RESET Framework and the New Governance Landscape
content.body:
From 1 April 2026, the UK government fundamentally changed how digital and technology governance works. The old spend control process — where GDS centrally approved line-by-line spending above certain thresholds — has been removed. In its place, the RESET framework establishes five principles that reshape the relationship between the centre and departments:

First, decisions should be delegated to those closest to delivery. This is a direct challenge to the old model where central committees made decisions about local technology choices. It means architecture governance within departments must become more capable and more accountable.

Second, the centre of government should focus on the biggest strategic risks and cross-cutting priorities. GDS no longer reviews every initiative above a threshold. Instead, it supports organisations with high-risk, novel, and complex initiatives — and those exceeding the organisation's Delegated Authority Limit.

Third, functional expertise should be embedded in departments and their arm's length bodies. This means architecture governance cannot rely on calling in central experts. Departments need their own architecture capability to run effective governance.

Fourth, approval of decisions should be done once and done well by those accountable. This attacks the old problem of the same decision being reviewed by multiple boards at multiple levels, each adding delay without adding insight.

Fifth, trust, openness and collaboration should be the foundation. The pipeline — managed through Government Assurance Services — gives central visibility of what departments are doing without requiring central approval for each item.

The practical implication for architecture governance is significant. Departments now have much greater autonomy — and much greater accountability. If your departmental governance is weak, there is no central safety net catching problems. The quality of your local architecture governance directly determines the quality of your technology outcomes.

content.heading: Designing Governance That Delivery Teams Actually Use
content.body:
The litmus test for governance is simple: do delivery teams engage with it voluntarily, or only when forced? If teams avoid your governance process, route around it, or present decisions after the fact, your governance has failed regardless of how well-designed it looks on paper.

Effective governance has several characteristics that distinguish it from bureaucratic governance:

It is proportionate. Not every decision needs a board review. Good governance defines clear thresholds: decisions below a certain significance are made within the team, decisions above it go to a design authority, and only the most significant or cross-cutting decisions escalate to the ARB. The Ministry of Justice Digital's approach — an early gateway requiring an overarching brief, a more in-depth second gateway, and a third gateway operating continuously — illustrates this layered model.

It is fast. If your governance process adds three weeks to a decision that should take three days, teams will stop using it. Set service levels for governance decisions. A lightweight review should take days, not weeks. If the board only meets fortnightly and requires two weeks of document preparation, you have built a month of delay into every significant decision.

It gives something back. The best governance processes do not just challenge — they add value. An architecture review that spots a reuse opportunity, identifies a risk the team had not considered, or connects the team to another programme doing similar work earns its place. Teams return to governance that helps them, not governance that merely judges them.

It is staffed by practitioners. Governance boards staffed entirely by people who have not designed or built anything recently lose credibility fast. Include working architects, technical leads, and security specialists who understand the reality of delivery alongside the strategic perspectives.

It adapts to context. A discovery-phase team exploring options needs different governance from a live-service team making a production change. A small internal tool needs different governance from a citizen-facing service processing millions of transactions. One-size-fits-all governance inevitably fits nothing well.

content.heading: The Architecture Review Board: Composition, Authority and Cadence
content.body:
The Architecture Review Board (or Design Authority — the name varies between departments) is the primary governance mechanism for architecture decisions within a department or programme. Getting it right requires careful thought about three dimensions: who sits on it, what authority it has, and how often it meets.

Composition should balance breadth with expertise. A typical effective ARB includes: the Chief Architect or Head of Architecture (chair), senior solution architects representing major programmes, the Head of Security or a senior security architect, a representative from the data architecture function, a representative from the enterprise architecture function, and optionally a delivery manager or product owner to represent the delivery perspective. Rotating guest members from specific programmes bring context for particular decisions.

Authority must be explicit and understood. The ARB needs to be clear about what it can decide, what it can recommend, and what it can escalate. Common authority models include:

Advisory only — the ARB provides recommendations but teams make final decisions. This works for mature teams but provides no backstop for poor decisions.

Approval authority — the ARB must approve certain categories of decision (technology selection, integration patterns, security architecture) before they proceed. This provides stronger governance but risks becoming a bottleneck.

Exception-based — teams proceed with decisions autonomously but must escalate if they cannot reach consensus, if the decision is cross-cutting, or if it deviates from established standards. This is the most agile-compatible model and aligns well with the RESET principle of delegating to those closest to delivery.

Cadence should match the pace of delivery. Many ARBs meet fortnightly, but this is a convention, not a requirement. Consider: a standing weekly slot (even if sometimes unused) for urgent decisions, a fortnightly deep-dive for complex reviews, and asynchronous review via written ADRs for straightforward decisions that do not require discussion. The goal is that governance never delays a decision by more than a few days.

content.heading: The Cross-Government ADR Framework
content.body:
In late 2025, the GDS Enterprise Architecture team published a formal Architectural Decision Record Framework for the public sector. This elevates ADRs from a team-level practice to a cross-government standard for ensuring visibility, traceability, and strategic alignment of technology decisions.

The framework serves the Technical Design Council — the body of empowered CTOs that makes decisions affecting cross-government architecture and shared platforms. ADRs are the mechanism through which decisions are proposed to, and recorded by, the TDC. But the framework applies equally to departmental and programme-level decisions.

The significance of this for governance is profound. Previously, architecture decisions were often invisible outside the team that made them. A department might choose a particular integration pattern without knowing that three other departments had already made the same choice — or a contradictory one. The ADR Framework creates a shared practice that makes decisions discoverable across government.

For your departmental governance, this means:

Adopt the cross-government ADR template as your standard. This ensures consistency and makes your decisions legible to others across government — and to the Enterprise Architecture team who may identify opportunities for reuse or coordination.

Define which decisions require ADRs in your governance framework. Not every choice needs one, but every architecturally significant decision should have a corresponding ADR. The framework is clear: ADRs are for decisions that affect how systems are structured, integrated, secured, or evolved.

Make ADRs the input to your governance process, not a separate bureaucratic exercise. When a team brings a decision to the ARB, they bring it as a draft ADR. The board's role is to review, challenge, and either accept or return it. The ADR then becomes the record of the governance outcome.

Use ADR status to track the lifecycle of governance decisions. Proposed ADRs are decisions awaiting governance review. Accepted ADRs are active policy. Superseded ADRs show how thinking evolved. This creates an auditable history that satisfies the transparency and accountability requirements of the Digital Assurance Playbook.

content.heading: Governance Anti-Patterns in Government
content.body:
Recognising governance anti-patterns helps you avoid them. These are common failure modes observed across government departments.

The Rubber Stamp Board meets regularly but never challenges anything. Teams present decisions already made, the board nods, and everyone leaves. This governance provides an illusion of oversight while adding no value. It exists because the board lacks the technical depth to challenge, or because its authority is unclear, or because it has never pushed back and teams have learned it is merely ceremonial.

The Ivory Tower Board is staffed by senior architects who have not delivered anything recently. They challenge based on theoretical best practice rather than practical delivery constraints. Teams find their recommendations impractical, ignore them, and the board's credibility erodes. The fix is including practitioners who understand the reality of delivery alongside the strategists.

The Bottleneck Board has more demand than capacity. It meets fortnightly but has a backlog of eight items. Teams wait weeks for decisions. Delivery slows. Teams start making decisions without governance approval because they cannot afford the delay. The fix is delegation: raise the threshold for what needs board review, empower architects to make decisions below that threshold, and use asynchronous ADR review for straightforward decisions.

The Scope Creep Board reviews things it should not. It comments on implementation details, coding standards, or UI design — things that belong to the delivery team. It conflates architecture governance with technical micromanagement. The fix is a clear terms of reference that defines exactly what the board reviews and what it does not.

The Shadow Governance problem occurs when the official governance is so burdensome that an informal, undocumented process emerges alongside it. Senior architects make decisions in corridor conversations. These decisions are never recorded, never challenged, and create an accountability gap. The fix is making official governance fast and lightweight enough that people prefer it to the informal alternative.

The Documentation Theatre Board requires extensive documentation before it will review anything — a full solution architecture document, a risk assessment, a cost model, and a stakeholder analysis — even for a simple technology choice. This creates a perverse incentive: teams either spend disproportionate effort on documentation or avoid governance entirely. The fix is proportionate documentation requirements: an ADR for simple decisions, a brief for moderate decisions, and a full architecture document only for the most significant ones.

content.heading: Integrating Governance with Agile Delivery
content.body:
Agile delivery and architecture governance are often presented as being in tension. They are not — but they require different governance patterns than traditional waterfall delivery.

In waterfall, governance happens at stage gates: approve the design before build begins, approve the build before testing begins. This works because decisions are made sequentially and upfront. In agile delivery, architecture decisions emerge iteratively. The team does not know all the answers at the start. Governance must accommodate this reality.

Effective governance patterns for agile delivery include:

Continuous engagement rather than stage gates. The architect is embedded in the delivery team (or closely aligned to it) and participates in sprint ceremonies. Architecture decisions are made as part of delivery, not in a separate process. The ARB receives regular updates and intervenes only when cross-cutting concerns arise.

Architecture runway. Significant architecture decisions are made slightly ahead of delivery, creating a runway of decided infrastructure and patterns that teams can build on. Governance reviews the runway decisions, which are typically ADRs, in a batch rather than blocking individual sprints.

Last responsible moment. Governance does not require all decisions upfront. It accepts that some decisions can be deferred until more information is available. The governance process defines which decisions must be made early (those that are expensive to reverse) and which can be deferred (those that are cheap to change).

Lightweight checkpoints aligned to delivery phases. In the GDS delivery model (discovery, alpha, beta, live), governance naturally aligns to phase transitions: a lightweight architecture brief at the end of discovery, a solution architecture at the start of beta, and operational readiness at the transition to live. These are not gates that block progress — they are points where the architecture is reviewed to ensure it remains sound.

The Digital Assurance Playbook explicitly states that assurance should be proportionate to risk and integrated with the organisation's overall assurance framework. This gives architects licence to design governance that fits their delivery model rather than imposing a separate bureaucratic process on top of agile delivery.

content.heading: Measuring Governance Effectiveness
content.body:
How do you know if your governance is working? You need metrics that measure both effectiveness (is governance improving outcomes?) and efficiency (is governance adding minimal friction?).

Effectiveness metrics include: the number of architecture decisions that were later reversed or caused problems (lower is better — governance should catch issues early), the degree of technology coherence across the estate (are teams making consistent choices?), the frequency of duplicated effort identified and prevented, and the alignment of delivery outcomes with strategic objectives.

Efficiency metrics include: the average time from a decision being submitted to governance to receiving a response, the number of decisions waiting in the governance backlog, team satisfaction with the governance process (survey annually), and the ratio of decisions approved without change versus those requiring rework.

Leading indicators that governance is failing include: teams consistently presenting decisions after implementation, increasing time-to-decision, declining attendance at governance forums, growing informal decision-making outside the process, and repeated escalations of the same types of decisions (indicating unclear delegation).

The Digital Assurance Playbook introduces a Digital Performance Framework that will track performance metrics at a departmental level. While the details are still emerging, this creates an environment where governance effectiveness will become more visible to senior leadership. Architecture governance that demonstrably improves delivery outcomes will be valued; governance that merely adds process will be challenged.

Practically, review your governance quarterly. Ask: what did we catch that would otherwise have been a problem? What did we slow down unnecessarily? What decisions are teams making without us that we should have been involved in? Use the answers to continuously calibrate your governance — tightening where risks are emerging, loosening where teams are mature and making good decisions independently.

workedExample.title: Redesigning Architecture Governance at DESNZ After RESET
workedExample.context: The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) has 14 digital services in various stages of delivery, supported by 6 agile delivery teams. Before April 2026, their architecture governance consisted of a monthly Architecture Review Board that reviewed all technology decisions above £100,000. The board was chaired by the Chief Architect and attended by senior architects from each programme. Under the old spend control regime, the board also prepared submissions for GDS approval. With the removal of central spend controls and the introduction of the Digital Assurance Playbook, the department needs to redesign its governance to reflect the new autonomy and accountability.
workedExample.approach:
The Lead Solution Architect is tasked with redesigning governance to align with RESET principles.

Week 1 — Assessment of Current State:
The architect reviews the last 12 months of ARB activity. They find: 60% of items were straightforward technology selections that could have been delegated to programme architects. 25% were genuinely cross-cutting decisions that benefited from board review. 15% were items presented after decisions had already been made, effectively rubber-stamping. Average time from submission to decision: 3.5 weeks. Team satisfaction survey score: 4.2 out of 10.

Week 2 — Designing the New Model:
The architect proposes a three-tier governance model:

Tier 1 (Team-level): Decisions that affect only one service and cost below £500,000. Made by the programme architect, recorded as an ADR using the cross-government template, and shared with the architecture community for awareness. No board review required.

Tier 2 (Design Authority): Decisions that affect multiple services, introduce new technology to the estate, or involve security architecture changes. Reviewed asynchronously by a rotating panel of three senior architects within 5 working days. Escalated to the full board only if the panel cannot reach consensus.

Tier 3 (Architecture Review Board): Cross-departmental decisions, decisions affecting the enterprise architecture, decisions with whole-life cost above £5 million (aligning with the pipeline threshold), and decisions escalated from Tier 2. Monthly meeting with the option for extraordinary sessions.

Week 3 — Pipeline Integration:
The architect works with the digital assurance team to align the governance tiers with the Government Assurance Services pipeline. Tier 3 decisions are automatically flagged on the pipeline. The architect creates an intranet page searchable as 'Digital and Technology Assurance' as required by the Playbook.

Week 4 — Rollout and Communication:
The architect presents the new model to all delivery teams, emphasising what has changed: most decisions are now faster, the ADR is the primary governance artefact, and the board exists to help rather than to block.
workedExample.outcome: After three months of the new model: average decision time drops from 3.5 weeks to 4 days for Tier 1 and 8 days for Tier 2. Team satisfaction rises to 7.1 out of 10. The ARB meets monthly but only reviews 3-4 genuinely cross-cutting decisions per session instead of 8-10 mixed items. Two reuse opportunities are identified through the shared ADR repository that would have been missed under the old model. The Digital Assurance Playbook's expectation of proportionate, risk-based assurance is met without creating a governance vacuum.
workedExample.lessonsLearned: The key insight was that most governance problems are caused by reviewing too many things at too high a level. By delegating routine decisions to the right level and making the ADR the governance currency, the architect reduced friction while increasing visibility. The cross-government ADR Framework provided a ready-made template that did not need to be invented locally. The RESET principles gave political cover for reducing central control — the redesign was aligned with government policy, not fighting against it.

civilServiceScenario.title: Governance Conflict Between Central and Departmental Architecture Teams
civilServiceScenario.background: A large department (8,000+ staff, 200+ digital professionals) has a mature architecture practice with its own Design Authority. However, the GDS Enterprise Architecture team has identified that the department's messaging platform choice conflicts with a cross-government decision being developed by the Technical Design Council. The department made its decision six months ago, has already begun implementation, and the programme is politically sensitive with ministerial interest. The TDC is proposing a different approach that would better support cross-government interoperability.
civilServiceScenario.challenge: You need to navigate the tension between departmental autonomy (a RESET principle) and cross-government coherence (an Enterprise Architecture team objective). The department's decision was made legitimately through its own governance. The TDC's emerging decision has cross-government strategic rationale. Neither side is wrong, but the positions are incompatible.
constraints: The department has already invested £800,000 in implementation of its chosen approach
The programme has ministerial visibility and a fixed launch date in four months
The TDC decision is still in draft and has not been formally ratified
The GDS Enterprise Architecture team has no direct authority over departmental decisions under RESET
The department's solution works well for its own needs but creates integration challenges for other departments
There is no established escalation path for conflicts between departmental and cross-government governance
The department's Chief Architect is supportive of cross-government alignment but faces internal pressure to deliver on time
civilServiceScenario.yourRole: You are the department's Lead Solution Architect. Your Chief Architect has asked you to assess the situation and recommend a path forward that respects both the department's delivery commitments and the cross-government direction.
civilServiceScenario.discussion:
This scenario tests the governance maturity that distinguishes senior architects. There is no clean answer. The options include: proceed with the departmental decision and accept the interoperability cost (pragmatic but creates technical debt), pause implementation and adopt the TDC direction (principled but delays a ministerial priority), or design an adapter layer that allows the department's choice to interoperate with the TDC standard (compromise but adds complexity and cost).

The governance lesson is about the relationship between levels. Under RESET, the department has autonomy — but the TDC exists precisely to handle cross-cutting decisions. The correct governance response is probably a formal ADR that acknowledges the conflict, documents the department's rationale for proceeding, commits to a migration path within a defined timeframe, and proposes the adapter pattern as an interim measure. This respects the TDC's strategic role while honouring the department's delivery commitment.

practiceArtefact.description: Design a three-tier architecture governance framework for a medium-sized government department (5 delivery teams, 12 digital services, 80 digital professionals). The framework should define: what decisions are made at each tier, who makes them, how quickly decisions must be reached, what documentation is required at each tier, how decisions are recorded and made visible, and how the framework integrates with the Digital Assurance Playbook's pipeline requirements.
practiceArtefact.guidance: Start from the RESET principles: delegate to those closest to delivery. Work upward from the team level, defining what genuinely needs escalation at each stage. Consider the cross-government ADR Framework as the documentation standard. Think about how your governance connects to the Government Assurance Services pipeline for initiatives above £5 million. Address the question of what happens when the governance process disagrees with the delivery team — what is the escalation path and who has final authority?
practiceArtefact.modelAnswer:
**Architecture Governance Framework — [Department Name]**

Effective from: [Date] | Owner: Chief Architect | Review: Quarterly

**Principles:**
1. Decisions are made at the lowest appropriate level
2. Governance adds value, not just process
3. Speed of decision is proportionate to reversibility
4. All architecturally significant decisions are recorded as ADRs
5. Governance is transparent — all decisions are visible to the architecture community

**Tier 1 — Team Decisions (target: same day)**
Scope: Decisions affecting a single service, within established patterns, below £500k
Decision maker: Programme Architect
Documentation: ADR using cross-government template
Visibility: Published to architecture Slack channel and ADR repository
Examples: Library selection within approved stack, internal API design, data model changes within service boundary

**Tier 2 — Design Authority Review (target: 5 working days)**
Scope: New technology introduction, cross-service integration, security architecture, deviation from standards
Decision maker: Rotating panel of 3 senior architects (async review, sync meeting if needed)
Documentation: ADR with options analysis
Visibility: Published to ADR repository, flagged to Chief Architect
Examples: New database technology, new integration pattern, authentication architecture for a new service

**Tier 3 — Architecture Review Board (monthly, extraordinary if urgent)**
Scope: Enterprise-wide decisions, initiatives above £5m (pipeline-aligned), cross-departmental impact, strategic technology direction
Decision maker: Chief Architect (chair) with board consensus
Documentation: Full ADR with cost/risk analysis, strategic alignment statement
Visibility: Published to ADR repository, recorded on Government Assurance Services pipeline
Examples: Platform selection, enterprise integration strategy, major technology migration, new shared service adoption

**Escalation:** If Tier 2 panel cannot reach consensus within 5 days, escalate to Tier 3. If Tier 3 identifies cross-government impact, escalate to TDC via GDS Enterprise Architecture team.

**Pipeline Integration:** All Tier 3 decisions are reflected in the Government Assurance Services pipeline. The digital assurance team is notified of all Tier 3 items to ensure alignment with broader assurance activity.

**Conflict Resolution:** If a delivery team disagrees with a governance decision, they may formally appeal to the Chief Architect within 5 days, providing evidence of why the decision should be reconsidered. The Chief Architect's decision is final.

reflectiveQuestions: Think about the governance processes in your current organisation. Would you classify them as enabling or blocking? What evidence supports your assessment?
How has the removal of central spend controls affected your department's architecture governance? Has more autonomy led to better decisions, or has it created gaps?
When was the last time your governance process identified a genuine problem that would otherwise have been missed? If you cannot think of an example, what does that tell you?
How would you handle a situation where your governance process recommended against a decision that a senior stakeholder was politically committed to?
Does your organisation use ADRs consistently? If not, what is preventing adoption, and what would you need to change in your governance process to make ADRs the default?

knowledgeCheck.question: Under the RESET framework introduced in April 2026, what replaced the old GDS spend control process?
options: A stricter approval process managed by HM Treasury
The Digital Assurance Playbook with devolved organisational assurance and pipeline reporting
No governance at all — departments are fully autonomous
An automated approval system that reviews spend algorithmically
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The RESET framework removed central spend controls and replaced them with the Digital Assurance Playbook. Organisations now own their own assurance and approvals, with GDS providing support for high-risk and complex initiatives. All initiatives above £5 million must be recorded on the Government Assurance Services pipeline.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the primary purpose of the Technical Design Council (TDC)?
options: To approve all technology spending across government
To make decisions affecting cross-government architecture and shared platforms
To conduct service assessments for new digital services
To manage the recruitment of architects across the civil service
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The TDC is made up of empowered CTOs from across the public sector and is responsible for decisions that affect cross-government architecture and shared platforms. It uses Architecture Decision Records as the mechanism for proposing and recording these decisions.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which governance model best aligns with the RESET principle of 'delegating decisions to those closest to delivery'?
options: All technology decisions reviewed by a central Architecture Review Board
Exception-based governance where teams decide autonomously and escalate only when necessary
Governance that requires full documentation before any decision can proceed
A single architect who approves all decisions for the department
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Exception-based governance delegates decision authority to delivery teams by default, with escalation only when decisions are cross-cutting, contentious, or exceed defined thresholds. This aligns with the RESET principle while still providing oversight for genuinely significant decisions.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the key indicator that architecture governance has failed?
options: The governance board occasionally rejects proposals
Teams present decisions to the board after implementation rather than before
The board requests changes to proposed architectures
Some decisions take more than one meeting to resolve
knowledgeCheck.explanation: When teams routinely present decisions after implementation, governance has become a rubber stamp rather than a genuine review process. Teams have concluded that governance adds delay without value, so they proceed without it. Occasional rejections and requested changes are signs that governance is working — it is catching genuine issues.

knowledgeCheck.question: Under the Digital Assurance Playbook, what is the pipeline reporting threshold for digital and technology initiatives?
options: £100,000 for digital, £1 million for technology
£1 million for all initiatives
£5 million whole life cost
£20 million for cross-government initiatives
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The Digital Assurance Playbook sets a £5 million whole life cost threshold for recording initiatives on the Government Assurance Services pipeline. This replaced the previous lower thresholds under the old spend control regime. Organisations may set their own lower internal thresholds appropriate to their context.
